did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 35 begins with Elihu continuing his response, presenting his words as an answer to Job and his friends.
Did you know? Elihu frames Job’s claim as a question: Can one say that human righteousness is greater than God’s righteousness? In this way, he emphasizes the difference between human beings and God.

Did you know? Elihu also mentions another claim attributed to Job: that righteousness offers no clear practical benefit and that sin makes no difference. The chapter addresses the significance of human actions before God.
Did you know? Elihu directs attention to the heavens and the high clouds to illustrate the vastness of the world and humanity’s limitations in comparison.
Did you know? According to Elihu, human sins do not harm God Himself, even when they are numerous. In this way, he distinguishes between sin’s effect on human beings and God’s relation to sin.
Did you know? Elihu concludes that a person’s wickedness or righteousness mainly affects other people: wickedness harms others, while righteousness benefits them.
Did you know? The chapter describes the oppressed crying out because of widespread oppression and violence, presenting their suffering as a harsh social reality.

Did you know? Elihu argues that the oppressed do not turn sufficiently to God, who is described as the One who gives songs in the night. This expression presents the night as a time when people can seek comfort and guidance.
Did you know? Elihu says that God teaches people through animals and the birds of the sky, presenting the natural world as a source of reflection and wisdom.
Did you know? At the end of the chapter, Elihu accuses Job of speaking many foolish words. This reflects Elihu’s critical view of Job’s words, not a neutral description of the chapter.
